courses.title: Biostatistics (BIO 208)
courses.description: Data types, descriptive statistics, probability and distributions, sampling, hypothesis testing and common statistical tests for health research.

topics.title: Data, Variables and Presentation
topics.summary: Types of variables, scales of measurement and tables and charts.

material.heading: Types of data
material.body: Qualitative (categorical) variables may be nominal (no order: blood group, sex, state of origin) or ordinal (ordered: pain score mild/moderate/severe, cancer stage). Quantitative (numerical) variables may be discrete (counts: number of children) or continuous (measurements: height, blood pressure, Hb). Scales of measurement are nominal, ordinal, interval (equal intervals, no true zero: temperature in °C) and ratio (true zero: weight, age).
keyPoints: Nominal: no order; ordinal: ordered categories
Ratio scale has a true zero

material.heading: Presenting data
material.body: Frequency tables summarise how often values occur. Bar charts (separate bars) and pie charts display categorical data; histograms (touching bars, area proportional to frequency) show continuous data; line graphs show trends over time; scatter plots show the relationship between two continuous variables; box plots show median, quartiles and outliers.
keyPoints: Scatter plot for two continuous variables

questions.explanation: Blood groups are categories with no natural order.

questions.stem: Number of antenatal visits is a ___ variable.
questions.explanation: Visits are counted in whole numbers.

questions.stem: Which scale has a true zero point?
questions.explanation: Ratio scales (e.g. weight) have an absolute zero.

questions.explanation: Birth weight is continuous; histograms show its distribution.

questions.stem: Stages of cancer (I, II, III, IV) are measured on a/an ___ scale.
questions.explanation: Stages have a meaningful order but unequal intervals.

questions.explanation: Scatter plots display two continuous variables.

questions.explanation: Equal intervals but 0 °C is not an absence of temperature.

questions.stem: In a histogram, the bars:
questions.explanation: Adjacent bars reflect the continuity of the data.

topics.title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
topics.summary: Mean, median, mode, range, variance, standard deviation and skewness.

material.heading: Central tendency
material.body: The mean is the arithmetic average (sum ÷ number); it uses all values but is affected by extreme values (outliers). The median is the middle value of ordered data (for an even number, the average of the two middle values); it is preferred for skewed data such as income or length of hospital stay. The mode is the most frequent value and the only measure for nominal data. In a positively (right) skewed distribution, mean > median > mode; in a negatively skewed distribution, mean < median < mode; in a symmetrical normal distribution all three are equal.

material.heading: Dispersion
material.body: Range = maximum − minimum. The interquartile range (Q3 − Q1) contains the middle 50% of data and suits skewed data. Variance is the average squared deviation from the mean; the standard deviation (SD) is its square root, in the original units. The coefficient of variation (SD ÷ mean × 100%) compares variability between different units. The standard error of the mean (SE = SD/√n) measures the precision of a sample mean.

topics.title: Probability and the Normal Distribution
topics.summary: Probability rules, the binomial and normal distributions, and z-scores.

material.heading: Probability
material.body: Probability ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Complement: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). The binomial distribution describes the number of successes in n independent trials with the same probability p (e.g. number of HbSS children in a family of AS × AS parents). The Poisson distribution describes counts of rare events in a fixed interval.
keyPoints: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) if mutually exclusive
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) if independent

material.heading: The normal distribution
material.body: The normal (Gaussian) distribution is symmetrical and bell-shaped, defined by its mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ). About 68% of values lie within ±1 SD, 95% within ±1.96 (≈ 2) SD and 99.7% within ±3 SD. A z-score = (x − μ)/σ gives how many SDs a value is from the mean. Many laboratory reference ranges are the mean ± 2 SD of healthy people, so 5% of healthy individuals fall outside the 'normal range'.

questions.explanation: Probability ranges from 0 to 1.

questions.stem: The probability that two AS parents have two consecutive HbSS children is:
questions.explanation: Independent events: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

questions.stem: In a normal distribution, about what percentage of values lie within ±2 SD of the mean?
questions.explanation: About 95% lie within ±1.96 SD.

The normal distribution is:
questions.explanation: It is symmetrical about the mean.

questions.explanation: Binomial describes counts of successes in n trials.

topics.title: Sampling and Estimation
topics.summary: Population and sample, sampling methods, sampling error and confidence intervals.

material.heading: Sampling methods
material.body: A population is the whole group of interest; a sample is a subset studied. Probability sampling gives every member a known chance of selection: simple random, systematic (every kth), stratified (random samples from subgroups such as LGAs or sexes), cluster (randomly selected groups such as villages or schools — used in national surveys like NDHS) and multistage sampling. Non-probability sampling includes convenience, purposive, quota and snowball sampling; it is quicker but prone to selection bias.

material.heading: Estimation
material.body: A statistic (e.g. sample mean) estimates a parameter (population mean). Sampling error is the difference due to chance and falls as sample size increases. A 95% confidence interval for a mean is approximately mean ± 1.96 × SE; it gives a range which, in repeated sampling, would contain the true population value 95% of the time. Wider intervals indicate less precision; larger samples give narrower intervals.

questions.explanation: Stratified sampling samples within defined subgroups.

questions.stem: Selecting every 10th patient from a clinic register is:
questions.explanation: Systematic sampling picks every kth unit.

questions.stem: Which is a non-probability sampling method?
questions.explanation: Convenience sampling does not give known selection probabilities.

questions.stem: Randomly selecting whole villages and studying everyone in them is:
questions.explanation: Cluster sampling selects groups rather than individuals.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for a mean is approximately:
questions.explanation: 95% CI ≈ mean ± 1.96 × standard error.

questions.stem: Increasing the sample size will:
questions.explanation: A larger n reduces the standard error.

questions.stem: A value calculated from a sample to estimate a population value is a:
questions.explanation: Statistics describe samples; parameters describe populations.

questions.stem: Sampling hidden populations by asking participants to refer others is:
questions.explanation: Snowball sampling grows through referrals.

topics.title: Hypothesis Testing and Statistical Tests
topics.summary: Null hypothesis, p-values, errors, and choosing t-tests, chi-square and correlation.

material.heading: Hypothesis testing
material.body: The null hypothesis (H0) states there is no difference or association; the alternative (H1) states there is. The p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed if H0 were true; p < 0.05 is conventionally 'statistically significant'. A Type I error (α) is rejecting a true H0 (false positive); a Type II error (β) is failing to reject a false H0 (false negative). Power = 1 − β, the ability to detect a real effect; it increases with sample size.
keyPoints: Type I = false positive (α); Type II = false negative (β)

material.heading: Choosing a test
material.body: Compare two means of independent groups with the independent (Student's) t-test; the same subjects before and after with the paired t-test; three or more means with ANOVA. Compare proportions or test association between categorical variables with the chi-square (χ²) test (Fisher's exact test when expected counts are small). Measure linear association between two continuous variables with Pearson's correlation coefficient r (−1 to +1); Spearman's rank correlation for ordinal or skewed data. Non-parametric alternatives include Mann–Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Correlation does not imply causation.
keyPoints: Two independent means → t-test; paired → paired t-test
